articles.title: A Pennsylvania family trust held about 65 properties; a son pointed to at least $10 million in rental income by 2022 when accusing his brother of mismanagement, but a November 12 court upheld dismissal of his case
articles.summary: A Pennsylvania court on Thursday upheld the dismissal of a man's case accusing his brother and others of mismanaging a family real estate trust and
articles.body: A Pennsylvania court on Thursday upheld the dismissal of a man's case accusing his brother and others of mismanaging a family real estate trust and diverting its income. Jacob Singer claimed that millions of dollars generated through rentals could not be accounted for. However, the court found that he had not produced enough evidence to prove that the money had been improperly taken.The Pennsylvania Superior Court rejected Jacob's challenge to an earlier ruling that dismissed his claims against his brother, David Singer, Michael Singer Inc., which operates as Michael Singer Real Estate, and the trust's former accountants. The court also found that Jacob had not established his right to take immediate control of the properties.According to the information available on Justia, the dispute centred on a real estate portfolio built by the family's patriarch, Michael Singer. He founded a property management company and accumulated income-generating properties. He later created trusts for his sons, including one for Jacob, whose trust document was signed in June 2005. Jacob was appointed trustee and given powers to manage its assets.Michael transferred most of his property portfolio into the trust. At the time of the proceedings, it appeared to hold around 65 properties outright, along with interests in about 23 others owned by separate entities. Jacob and Michael had been involved in managing the properties. Jacob said he had authorised his father to look after those he did not manage himself.The disagreement grew after Jacob came to believe that David and the family company had taken over the properties without his authority. He also questioned how rental earnings and payments linked to the properties were handled. In July 2022, he filed a lawsuit seeking financial records, control of the properties and relief over the alleged wrongdoing.Why Jacob claimed millions were missingJacob said he had asked David and the property management company for records and the transfer of management responsibilities. He also sought financial information from the trust's accountants, Kirk Eldridge and Mazars USA LLP. He alleged that the parties did not provide all the information he wanted and later removed the accountants from their role.He also claimed that several trust properties were not being maintained as well as those connected to David or David's trust. Jacob suspected that the trust had overpaid on promissory notes issued to Michael and that income due to it had been diverted.A key part of his case was the difference between rental income and the money visible in a bank account. Jacob claimed the trust had earned at least $10 million in rental income by the end of 2022, but the account balance did not reflect that amount. He argued that David had moved the money into accounts under his control.The court found that this comparison did not prove that funds had been misappropriated. Jacob had not produced records showing the account's deposits and withdrawals or where the withdrawn money had gone. He was also unable to provide a clear calculation of the losses.The defendants had submitted an expert report disputing Jacob's belief that all promissory notes had been repaid. It said an outstanding balance remained. Jacob did not appoint an expert to support his claims. The court agreed that specialist financial knowledge was needed to examine the accounts of a trust holding dozens of rental properties.Court rejects demand for an accountingJacob also sought an independent examination of the trust's financial records. The court said that although a party can ask for an accounting as a form of relief, this does not automatically create a legal right to one. Such a right must arise from another valid claim, such as a breach of contract.Since Jacob had not established the underlying claims needed to support his request, the court found no basis to order an accounting. It also said the alleged discovery violations did not independently give him that right.Jacob had separately argued that the defendants withheld important records. The trial court had ordered them to provide further information in 2023 and April 2024, subject to confidentiality restrictions. It also allowed parties to seek sanctions if the orders were not followed.However, Jacob did not file further discovery applications or seek sanctions before discovery closed. The Superior Court said he could not later complain that the trial court had failed to enforce its directions when he had not raised the continuing dispute in time.Why Jacob could not take control of the propertiesJacob argued that, as trustee, he had the authority to manage the properties and that David and the company had no legal basis to retain control. The defendants produced property management agreements signed by Michael, naming him and/or the family company as agents responsible for managing rental properties. Some agreements included automatic renewal provisions.Jacob challenged these agreements during his appeal, arguing that they had been signed before the properties were transferred to the trust and that licensing issues made them unenforceable. But he had not raised these objections when the agreements were submitted during the summary judgment proceedings. The court said he had raised them too late.The judges also found no evidence showing when Michael stopped managing the properties or how David and the company had wrongfully taken over that responsibility. They rejected the argument that alleged violations of Pennsylvania's real estate licensing law automatically made the agreements invalid.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Ariana Grande turns years of private charity into a formal foundation, donates $125,000 to transgender crisis hotline and introduces an unusual concert fundraising strategy to support local nonprofits
articles.summary: For much of her career, Ariana Grande's charitable contributions have happened away from the spotlight.
articles.body: For much of her career, Ariana Grande's charitable contributions have happened away from the spotlight. The singer has supported children's hospitals, helped transgender young people and directed money towards reproductive health organisations, often without making a public announcement. As reported by the Associated Press, that approach has begun to change with the launch of her Brighter Days Ahead Foundation in May 2026. The initiative brings several years of individual donations and advocacy under one organisation, with a focus on issues that Grande has spoken about publicly. It also reflects a changing approach to celebrity philanthropy, where fundraising, public influence and long-term support for smaller organisations increasingly overlap.Ariana Grande's years of charitable giving before launching her foundationGrande's charitable work did not begin with the foundation. Reportedly, over the years, she has made regular contributions to Royal Manchester Children's Hospital in England, donated proceeds from performances to nonprofit organisations and supported campaigns addressing the needs of transgender communities. Some of her contributions were deliberately kept private. In one instance, she anonymously helped fund a holiday gift drive for transgender young people.In 2022, she also launched a fundraising initiative that raised $3 million for transgender youth. Her donations to Planned Parenthood, including approximately $250,000 from concert proceeds in 2019, came at a time when abortion restrictions were being introduced in several American states.The creation of Brighter Days Ahead gives these activities a more permanent structure. The foundation intends to concentrate on LGBTQ+ rights, reproductive healthcare, immigrant rights and mental health, areas that have featured in Grande's public advocacy over several years.Her philanthropic adviser, Shauna Nep, said the decision came against a difficult backdrop for organisations working in these fields. Support for some of the causes Grande backs has weakened, while the groups dealing directly with affected communities face growing demands. Nep has worked with the singer since 2018 and encouraged her to move towards a more organised approach to charitable giving.Grande had reservations about establishing a formal foundation. According to Nep, the singer was concerned that such a move could create the impression that she was trying to build a public identity around philanthropy rather than her work as an artist.How Ariana Grande is turning concert venues into fundraising platformsThe foundation has also found a way to connect Grande's music career with its fundraising activities. During her Eternal Sunshine Tour, which began in 2026, the singer is using concert venues to introduce audiences to nonprofit organisations working in the cities she visits.The participating groups appear on large arena screens during the pre-show countdown. Fans can learn about their work and contribute to the foundation, with donors also receiving an opportunity to enter a sweepstake for a chance to attend the final concert in London.The arrangement allows fundraising to take place without significantly changing the concert experience. Nep said the intention was to bring charitable organisations into an environment where fans were already gathered, rather than asking audiences to step away from the event.Money raised through the tour will be divided among the local organisations featured at different stops. However, the foundation had not distributed any of these tour proceeds at the time of the report. Grants announced before then had come entirely from Grande's personal contributions, according to a foundation spokesperson.Ariana Grande donates $125,000 to transgender crisis support organisationAmong the organisations benefiting from Grande's contributions is Trans Lifeline, a nonprofit that operates a crisis hotline for transgender people. As reported by the Associated Press, the group has received a total of $125,000 from the singer, including $75,000 in emergency assistance in June 2025 and a further $50,000 when Brighter Days Ahead was formally launched in May 2026.The contribution helped the organisation restart a microgrants programme through which $100,000 was distributed directly to transgender people across the United States. Five grassroots organisations worked with Trans Lifeline to deliver the programme. Part of the funding was also used to improve benefits for employees providing direct crisis support.For organisations that depend heavily on individual contributions, celebrity involvement can bring more than financial assistance. Dante Alviar Horton, executive director of Trans Lifeline, said public attention from well-known supporters had helped the nonprofit maintain visibility and reach potential donors.He also pointed to the response to the Protect the Dolls T-shirt campaign, developed with designer Conner Ives. The initiative raised more than $500,000, with celebrities including Pedro Pascal helping draw attention to the message by wearing the shirts publicly.Why Grande chose the Entertainment Industry Foundation to manage her charityBrighter Days Ahead operates as a fiscally sponsored project of the Entertainment Industry Foundation, a public charity established in 1942 to support philanthropic initiatives connected to the entertainment industry. The arrangement provides a framework for collecting donations and directing grants without requiring Grande to build an entirely independent charitable organisation from scratch.The same structure has been used by other entertainers, including Charlize Theron and Olivia Rodrigo, to establish and manage philanthropic projects. The foundation has four funds, with Protect and Defend being its largest. It supports organisations involved in legal and legislative work concerning transgender young people, immigrants and reproductive rights.Nep said several of the grassroots organisations receiving support have limited access to institutional and government funding. Some have come to depend on contributions from the foundation as one of their major sources of financial assistance.Celebrity philanthropy has changed with the reach of social mediaGrande's foundation also reflects how the relationship between entertainers and charitable causes has shifted. Earlier generations of celebrities often relied on television interviews, newspapers and public appearances to draw attention to organisations they supported. Social media has given contemporary artists a more direct way to communicate with millions of followers.Genevieve Shaker, who teaches celebrity philanthropy and fundraising leadership at Indiana University's Lilly Family School of Philanthropy, said entertainers now have their own channels for sharing information about charitable work. The influence can extend beyond the celebrity's own financial contributions. There has also been scepticism about celebrity-led charitable initiatives, particularly when public advocacy appears to be disconnected from substantial financial commitments or sustained involvement. Grande's earlier reluctance to establish a foundation was partly shaped by concerns about how such work might be perceived, Nep said.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.body: MUMBAI: For the first time in recent years, Mumbai hosted an event on Sunday to honour a Pakistani scientist. The occasion was the birth centenary of Nobel laureate Abdus Salam and the event was an online lecture by eminent nuclear physicist Pervez Amirali Hoodbhoy, who spoke from Islamabad.The presentation, “The Truth About Abdus Salam: Science, Faith moved to and the Atom Bomb,’’ was organised by the Mumbai sub-regional council of the Indian Association of Physics Teachers. Raman and Jagdishchandra Bose,’’ he said.Hoodbhoy, a decorated scientist himself – a recipient of the Fulbright award in 1998 and the UNESCO Kalinga Prize in 2001 – said Salam played a key role in the initial years of research under former prime minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto as Pakistan began work to develop nuclear weapons.’’Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: A California woman and her newborn son died after she was discharged from hospital with signs of preeclampsia; seven years later, a jury awarded her family $9.25 million, but an old law limits their recovery
articles.summary: A family waited seven years for a jury to decide whether a doctor's negligence contributed to the deaths of a young mother and her newborn son.
articles.body: A family waited seven years for a jury to decide whether a doctor's negligence contributed to the deaths of a young mother and her newborn son. In California, 23-year-old Demi Dominguez died in April 2019 after being discharged from hospital with symptoms of a serious pregnancy complication. Her baby, Malakhi De Leon, also died shortly after an emergency delivery. On October 21, 2026, a jury found former obstetrician-gynecologist Arthur Park negligent and awarded the two families a combined $9.25 million. However, an older California medical malpractice law means they cannot collect the full amount.According to a verdict announcement published by patient advocacy organisation Consumer Watchdog, the jury awarded $3 million to Dominguez's mother, Tracy Dominguez, and $6.25 million to Malakhi's father, Xavier De Leon. The decision followed a trial in Kern County, Bakersfield, concerning the medical care provided before the deaths.Woman discharged after showing signs of preeclampsiaAccording to Consumer Watchdog's account of the case, Dominguez was eight months pregnant when she began experiencing symptoms including swelling, high blood pressure and blurred vision. Concerned about her condition, she sought medical attention at Mercy Southwest Hospital in Bakersfield.Park was the obstetrician-gynecologist responsible for her hospital care. Dominguez reportedly told him about her elevated blood pressure and swelling, but her concerns were not adequately addressed. She remained in hospital overnight for observation but was discharged without being diagnosed with preeclampsia, a potentially life-threatening pregnancy complication characterised by high blood pressure and signs of organ damage.She was instructed to follow up with her regular doctor. However, after her discharge, she visited her regular doctor and was sent home again without a diagnosis. Her condition deteriorated, and she suffered a seizure and died on April 19, 2019. After her death, an emergency Caesarean section was performed to deliver her son, Malakhi. The newborn was critically ill and was eventually transferred to another hospital for further treatment. Despite medical efforts, he died shortly after birth.Preeclampsia can develop during pregnancy and, without appropriate treatment, progress to eclampsia, which involves potentially fatal seizures. The family's case centred on whether the warning signs should have led to further monitoring and treatment before Dominguez was discharged.Jury finds former doctor negligentThe wrongful-death case took seven years to reach trial. During the proceedings, the family's legal team presented evidence concerning Dominguez's symptoms and the medical attention she received. They argued that the doctor had failed to recognise and respond appropriately to signs of preeclampsia. Park, who represented himself during the trial, argued that stress could raise blood pressure and that he had not been informed of the patient's concerning readings.The jury ultimately found Park negligent in his care of Dominguez and awarded compensation to her mother and the baby's father for their losses. Tracy received $3 million for the loss of her daughter, while Xavier was awarded $6.25 million for the loss of his son. The combined verdict amounted to $9.25 million.The family's lead attorney, Courtney Rowley, said after the verdict that the family had campaigned for changes to the law despite knowing they would not benefit from the reforms. She said, “This family fought so hard for a law to update the medical negligence caps which would not affect them.”Old California law limits family's compensationDespite the verdict, the family faces a significant restriction under California's Medical Injury Compensation Reform Act, commonly known as MICRA. At the time the lawsuit was filed in 2019, the law limited non-economic damages in medical malpractice cases to $250,000. These damages cover losses such as emotional suffering, loss of companionship and the absence of a loved one, rather than measurable financial expenses.California subsequently passed Assembly Bill 35 in 2022, increasing the limits on non-economic damages in medical negligence cases. However, the changes took effect on January 1, 2023, and do not apply retroactively to lawsuits filed before that date. As a result, the non-economic damages in the Dominguez and De Leon families' case remain subject to the older $250,000 limit despite the jury's substantially larger award.The families had also campaigned for changes to the law, knowing that the reforms would not benefit their own case. Their efforts were intended to help other families affected by medical negligence. The verdict therefore represents a significant legal milestone for the two families, but the old damages cap means the compensation they can recover remains far below the amount awarded by the jury.You use AI every day. articles.title: What Is a Teaser Bet? How Teasers Work in Football and Basketball Betting
articles.summary: A teaser bet moves the point spread or total in your favor on two or more games. Learn how teasers work, what they pay and when a 6 point NFL teaser makes sense.
articles.body: A teaser bet is when you get to pair two or more plays and adjust the line in one way or another. Bettors use a teaser to give themselves a better price on a play without having to take as big of a risk on covering a spread or total. In exchange for being able to adjust the line, you are paying the book different prices. This will guide you through how to make a teaser bet and what things you should consider before placing the wager. Teasers are offered in football and basketball only, because those are the sports where points scored come in predictable chunks. You will not find a teaser on a baseball or hockey card. What Is a Teaser Bet? A teaser bet is a type of parlay that lets you adjust the point spread or total on every leg by a fixed number of points. In football, the standard teaser is six points. In basketball, it is four. Every leg moves by the same amount and in your favor, and every leg has to win for the ticket to cash. The trade-off is the price. A standard two-team point spread parlay pays about +260. A two-team six-point teaser pays somewhere between -110 and -120 depending on the sportsbook. You are paying for the points with the odds. Teasers come in a few standard sizes: How Does a Teaser Bet Work? Start with the standard lines, then move each one by the teaser amount in the direction that helps your side. Favorites get smaller, underdogs get bigger, overs get lower, and unders get higher. Six Point NFL Teaser Example Suppose you like two Sunday favorites, but both spreads feel like a touchdown too many. A two-team six-point teaser turns them into this: Teasing a Total Totals work the same way. A game total of 47.5 becomes 41.5 if you tease the over or 53.5 if you tease the under. You can mix spreads and totals on the same ticket, but most books will not let you tease both sides of the same game. Four Point NBA Teaser Example Teaser Bet vs Parlay A teaser is a parlay with a discount on the lines and a discount on the payout. The question is which discount is bigger. The parlay pays about three times as much, so the teaser only makes sense when the extra six points raise your win probability enough to cover that gap. In NFL betting that happens in one specific spot, covered below. How Are Teaser Payouts Calculated? Unlike a standard parlay, a teaser payout is not calculated leg by leg. Each sportsbook publishes a fixed price for each number of legs at each teaser size. The table below shows the most common football prices. Books vary from 10 to 20 cents, so check the ticket before you confirm. To work out a payout, treat the whole teaser as one bet at the listed price. A $50 three team six point teaser at +170 returns $85 in profit plus your $50 stake. A $50 two team teaser at -120 returns $41.67 in profit. When Does a Teaser Bet Make Sense? A teaser earns its price when the six points move a spread across the two most common NFL margins of victory: 3 and 7. Games are decided by exactly 3 points roughly 15 percent of the time and by exactly 7 points close to 9 percent of the time, so a line that starts on one side of those numbers and finishes on the other picks up a large share of outcomes. The Wong Teaser The pattern has a name. In 2001, Stanford Wong described the two spots where a six-point teaser is historically profitable: Sportsbooks know this. Many now price two team teasers at -130 or -140, or shade the lines on exactly these games, which has thinned the edge. The logic still holds, but the margin is smaller than it was. When a Teaser Does Not Make Sense Teasers on College Football College spreads are larger and scores are more variable than in the NFL, so key numbers matter less. A six-point college teaser is usually a worse bet than the same teaser on an NFL card, even on a marquee SEC game. How to Place a Teaser Bet Not every app offers teasers on every game. Fanatics and bet365 build teasers from the bet slip, while FanDuel and BetMGM have a separate Teaser section on the NFL page. Our guide to the best sports betting apps compares every book. Common Teaser Betting Mistakes Responsible Gambling Sports betting should stay entertainment. Set a budget before you start, treat losses as the cost of that entertainment, and never chase them. Every legal sportsbook offers deposit limits, time limits, cool-off periods and self-exclusion in its account settings. If betting stops being fun, help is free and confidential: Teaser Bet FAQs What is a teaser bet in simple terms? A teaser is a parlay where every point spread or total is moved in your favor by a set number of points, usually six in football and four in basketball. All legs must win, and the payout is lower than a standard parlay because of the extra points. How much does a two-team six-point teaser pay? Most sportsbooks price a two-team six-point football teaser between -110 and -120, so a $110 to $120 stake wins $100. Some books charge -130 or more, so always check the ticket. What is a Wong teaser? A Wong teaser is a six-point NFL teaser that moves favorites of 7.5 to 8.5 down below 3, or underdogs of 1.5 to 2.5 up past 7. It is named for Stanford Wong, who showed these legs historically win often enough to beat the teaser price. Can you tease a total? Yes. A teaser moves a total by the same number of points as a spread, lowering the over or raising the under. Most bettors stick to spreads because totals do not cluster around key numbers. What happens if one leg of a teaser pushes? At most sportsbooks a push drops the teaser to the next lower number of legs. A two team teaser with one push becomes a single straight bet. Sweetheart teasers often count a push as a loss, so read the rules. Are teasers a good bet? Most are not. Six point NFL teasers that cross 3 and 7 are the exception and have a small historical edge. Teasers on big favorites, totals or basketball usually favor the sportsbook. Can you tease a moneyline? No. Teasers only apply to point spreads and totals. Moneylines have no number to move.

articles.title: What Is a Prop Bet? Player Props, Team Props and Game Props Explained
articles.summary: A prop bet is a wager on something inside a game other than the final result, like a player's yards or the first touchdown scorer. Learn how props work and how they are priced.
articles.body: A prop bet is a wager on a specific statistic to happen in the event that doesn’t depend on who wins or loses the game. There are many types of prop markets, and the most common are in football. For example, you could wager on the running back’s rushing yards, or which team (and how) will score score first. Props are some of the most extensive games available in the market and they continue to expand with more options provided on every game. Prop bets are usually how most people build same-game parlays. What Is a Prop Bet? A prop bet, short for proposition bet, is a wager on a specific outcome inside a game rather than on the final score. The team can lose, and your prop can still win. Sportsbooks post hundreds of props on a single NFL game and dozens on a regular season NBA or MLB game. Props fall into three groups: Most props are either over/under lines on a number or yes/no markets on an event. A few, like first touchdown scorer, list every eligible player at a different price. How Do Prop Bets Work? A prop works like a small bet on a small game. The sportsbook projects a number, sets a line at or near it, and attaches a price to each side. You pick a side, and the result settles on the official box score. Over/Under Player Prop Example Yes/No Prop Example Multi Option Prop Example Prop Settlement Rules Prop Bets vs Standard Bets The table explains why experienced bettors spend so much time on props. The lines are softer because the sportsbook cannot model every player in every game as carefully as it models the point spread. That cuts both ways: the book charges more juice to protect itself. How Are Prop Bet Odds Set and Paid? A player prop line starts with a projection. The sportsbook's model estimates the player's expected yards, points or receptions from recent usage, opponent, pace and game script. The line sits near the projection, usually at half point to avoid pushes. Both sides open around -115, and the book moves the line or the price as money comes in. Payouts use standard American odds. At -115, you risk $115 to win $100. At +110, you risk $100 to win $110. The implied probability of -115 is about 53.5 percent, so the two sides of a prop together add up to about 107 percent. That extra 7 percent is the hold, and it is higher than the 4.5 percent hold on a standard -110 spread. Alternate Lines Most apps let you move a prop line up or down for a different price. Goff over 245.5 at -115 might become over 275.5 at +160 or over 215.5 at -200. Alternate lines turn one prop into a ladder of choices and feed most same game parlay builders. Types of Prop Bets by Sport NFL Prop Bets NBA Prop Bets MLB Prop Bets Novelty and Special Event Props The Super Bowl brings props on the coin toss, the length of the national anthem, the Gatorade color and the first song of the halftime show. Most state regulators allow only props tied to on field play, so the famous novelty markets are mostly a Nevada and offshore phenomenon. Legal apps in most states offer game and player props on the Super Bowl but not entertainment props. Prop Betting Rules and Restrictions Prop markets have drawn the most regulatory attention of any bet type, because a single player can influence a single stat more easily than a final score. How to Find Value in Prop Bets How to Place a Prop Bet Every book in our best sports betting apps guide offers player and game props on all major leagues. bet365 and FanDuel typically post the deepest NFL prop menus, while Fanatics and theScore Bet focus on the most popular markets. Common Prop Betting Mistakes Responsible Gambling Sports betting should stay entertainment. Set a budget before you start, treat losses as the cost of that entertainment, and never chase them. Every legal sportsbook offers deposit limits, time limits, cool-off periods and self-exclusion in its account settings. If betting stops being fun, help is free and confidential: Prop Bet FAQs What does prop bet mean? Prop is short for proposition. A prop bet is a wager on a specific event or statistic inside a game, such as a player's yards or the first team to score, rather than on the final result. What is a player prop? A player prop is a bet on one athlete's performance, usually as an over/under on a stat line like passing yards, points or strikeouts, or as a yes/no on an event like scoring a touchdown. What is the difference between a prop bet and a parlay? A prop bet is a single wager on one event. A parlay combines two or more bets into one ticket. Props are often used as the legs of a same game parlay. What happens to a player prop if the player does not play? At most sportsbooks the prop is voided and the stake is returned. If the player is active but records no stats, the prop usually stands as a loss on the over. Check the house rules. Are prop bets good value? Props have softer lines than spreads but carry more juice, usually -115 or worse on both sides. They reward bettors who follow usage and injuries closely and punish casual guesses. Can you bet college player props? It depends on the state. Ohio and Maryland prohibit props on individual college athletes, New Jersey blocks bets on in-state college teams, and Kentucky has no college restriction. College team props and game props remain available wherever college betting is legal. What is an anytime touchdown scorer bet? It is a yes/no prop on whether a player scores at least one touchdown at any point in the game, including overtime. Rushing, receiving and return touchdowns all count. Do prop bets include overtime? Full game props include overtime unless the market name specifies a quarter or half. First half and quarter props end when that period ends.

articles.title: A Pennsylvania mother said her son's father pushed into her home and frightened their seven-year-old during a custody handoff; a November 12 appeals court upheld a three-year order barring contact with both
articles.summary: A routine child handoff in Pennsylvania turned into a frightening confrontation after a father allegedly pushed his way into his former partner's home and
articles.body: A routine child handoff in Pennsylvania turned into a frightening confrontation after a father allegedly pushed his way into his former partner's home and began shouting in front of their seven-year-old son. The mother said the boy became so distressed that he later begged her not to make him go with his father again. She also refused to let the child leave with him, saying she feared for his safety.The incident took place on June 23, when Daniel E Vaxter arrived at Amy M Lord's home to take their son to a kickboxing class. Lord later approached a court for protection, describing the confrontation and alleging that Vaxter had behaved aggressively towards her and the child.A Pennsylvania court granted her request and barred Vaxter from contacting both of them for three years. Vaxter challenged the order, arguing that the evidence did not establish abuse. However, the Pennsylvania Superior Court upheld the restriction on November 12, allowing the protection order to remain in place.According to the details available in the judgement, the events leading to the confrontation had started earlier that day with an argument over the boy's half-brother. Lord told the court that Vaxter was angry because she was encouraging their son to maintain contact with his sibling. She said he shouted at her during a phone call and refused to change his tone when she asked him to stop.The disagreement continued when he arrived at her home at around 4.50 pm. Lord said she opened the door and told him that their son would come out shortly. Instead, she alleged, Vaxter pushed his way inside and began shouting about court papers and the half-brother's biological mother.Their son heard the argument and came downstairs. Lord said the boy sat on the couch while his father continued shouting. She asked Vaxter to leave because she did not want him arguing inside the house in front of the child.Mother refuses to send son with fatherVaxter eventually went outside and called the boy to join him. The child followed him towards the car, but Lord became concerned about letting him leave.She told the court that Vaxter smelled strongly of marijuana and appeared to be under the influence of something. She was uncomfortable with their son travelling in his car in that condition.Lord called the child back. She alleged that Vaxter suddenly turned towards them and moved quickly in their direction. She became frightened, hugged the boy and placed him behind her before asking him to return inside.The mother said Vaxter then began recording the exchange on his phone. She alleged that his manner changed once he started filming, although he continued arguing outside the house. The confrontation ended when a landscaper arrived at the property. Vaxter got into his car and left.But the incident continued to affect the child after his father had gone. Lord said the boy was crying and extremely upset when they returned inside. He then told her, "Mommy please don't make me go with him anymore."Lord also told the court that her fear was not based only on that day's confrontation. She described earlier incidents in which Vaxter had allegedly thrown her against a wall when their son was six months old. She also accused him of hitting the child on the leg and hand on separate occasions.She said shouting and aggressive behaviour had been recurring problems. According to her testimony, the boy regularly told her that he was afraid of his father.Lord acknowledged that Vaxter had not physically touched her during the June 23 incident. However, she said his behaviour that day made her fear that he could become violent.Father disputes mother's accountVaxter gave a different version of what happened at the house. He said he had arrived to collect his son and entered after Lord opened the door. He acknowledged that they argued about the child's half-brother but claimed the disagreement escalated because Lord objected to his tone.He also disputed the mother's description of his behaviour outside the house. Vaxter submitted a video recording of the confrontation, saying he had started filming after Lord accused him of being abusive.The footage showed both parents arguing on the porch, with Lord standing close to the child and keeping him behind her. Vaxter could be heard accusing her of playing games and lying. He also called her "Karen" during the exchange.Vaxter relied on the recording to challenge the protection order. He argued that it showed no physical assault, threats or other conduct that could justify the mother's claims. He also pointed out that she had admitted there was no physical contact between them during the incident.However, the appeals court noted that the recording did not capture the entire confrontation. It began after the events inside the house, which meant it could not establish what had happened before Vaxter took out his phone.The lower court had accepted the mother's account of his behaviour before the recording began, including his entry into the house and his alleged movement towards her and the child.Court keeps father away from mother and child The dispute reached the Pennsylvania Superior Court after Vaxter challenged the protection order issued on July 2. He argued that the lower court had wrongly restricted his contact with his son and had not established that he posed a direct risk to the child.The appeals court did not agree. It said a protection order under Pennsylvania law does not require proof of actual physical injury. Evidence that a person was placed in reasonable fear of imminent serious bodily injury can be sufficient.In this case, the judges considered the mother's account of the confrontation along with her description of earlier alleged abuse. They found that the lower court had sufficient grounds to grant protection to both her and the child.The court also declined to reconsider the lower court's assessment of the witnesses. articles.title: US colleges struggle as international students turn away
articles.summary: Schools are experiencing steep enrollment declines for foreign students due to President Donald Trump’s efforts to curtail visas and employment.
articles.body:
The U.S. has long been a prime landing spot for international students. Thanks to President Donald Trump's visa crackdown, they're now taking their talents and tuition dollars elsewhere.

Tighter visa restrictions, stricter vetting and visa interview and appointment bottlenecks are contributing to what early data suggests will be a steep decline in international student enrollment nationwide this fall. And that was before Trump elevated Stephen Miller — the architect of his immigration agenda and campaign against academia — to chief of staff.

The limits on foreign students advances two administration aims: narrowing avenues of potential immigration and hitting the bank accounts of academic institutions conservatives have long criticized. Now, the policy changes, coupled with the administration's "America First" rhetoric and immigration sweeps, are taking hold, higher education leaders say.

"This is great for the United States that they're spending money here, that they're learning about our culture and our country," Michael Roth, president of Wesleyan University, a private liberal arts school, said of international students. "To just make it harder in the name of some kind of nationalism, it seems like we're shooting ourselves in the foot just to see how good our boots are."

The nationwide enrollment stats for the last academic year are expected to be released this month, but figures released by individual universities signify what is likely to be another slump this fall.

The number of international students enrolled at the University of Washington's Seattle campus declined for a second year in a row , falling to its lowest level in at least a decade. At The Ohio State University, those numbers fell by nearly 13% — the fewest it's seen in 16 years . And the Illinois Institute of Technology plans to borrow up to $200 million from its endowment because of its declining international student enrollment.

Benjamin Johnson, a spokesperson for Ohio State, said in a statement the university's international student enrollment "strengthens the academic experience" for all of their students.

"We want the world's best and brightest to choose Ohio State for school and stay to build a life and career in Ohio," Johnson said.

Stan Veuger, an economist at the American Enterprise Institute, a conservative-leaning think tank, said the Trump administration's goal is to "cut off all forms of migration to the maximum extent they can."

And with Miller now serving as the president's top adviser, "I think it will gradually get worse unless some of the Democrats manage to effectively push back," he said, referencing the pending Democratic takeover of Congress.

Higher education leaders warn that the administration's ever-changing visa rules and proposed restrictions could permanently damage the country's appeal to international talent and upend universities' finances. International students, who often pay full tuition, are an important source of revenue for colleges and sometimes subsidize financial aid and other services for domestic students.

"The latest data we have shows that when it comes to bachelor's degree programs at public universities, every international student opens up two spots for American students," said Zuzana C. Wootson, deputy director of federal policy at the Presidents' Alliance , which represents 500 presidents and chancellors of public and private colleges and universities.

"At the end of the day, who's going to be feeling the harm the most will be domestic students and Americans," she added.

House Education and Workforce Chair Tim Walberg argued the administration's policies ultimately benefit domestic students.

"For the present time, they're helping make sure that the schools are there for who they're supposed to be for," he said. "When we ultimately find out that we are woefully absent with people in the seats and there are plenty of places available for American students that meet the qualifications, then I think we can start to look at the international."

At Denison University in Ohio, President Adam Weinberg said his school is getting questions from concerned parents of foreign students because of all the policy changes. He said it's too early to tell what their foreign enrollment will look like, but "we expect pretty steep declines." International students make up 17% of the private liberal arts school's student body .

"I am absolutely in favor of immigration control and making sure that we're following our laws," Weinberg said. "And we absolutely need to educate U.S. students … colleges and universities should be educating them and preparing them to drive the economy forward. But we're also going to need to attract talent from around the world and we need to keep it."

The Trump administration's immigration policies and its enforcement mechanisms have "spread a great deal of fear and a great deal of anxiety" among international students, faculty on visas and undocumented students, said Patricia McGuire, president of Trinity Washington University, where international students make less than 2 percent of its enrollment.

McGuire said one of her international students was assaulted near a D.C. metro station and didn't call for help because "she was afraid if she called the police that she would be arrested and deported."

"That is just disgraceful for this country," she said.

Department of Homeland Security and top administration officials, including Vice President JD Vance, last month argued the stricter policies are designed to discourage visa fraud and that Americans should not have to compete against international students for work.

"The performative outrage is incredible," an unnamed DHS spokesperson said in a statement. "Where was the outrage when foreign nationals were abusing the system, violating the terms of their student visas, and making a mockery of our immigration laws? If the media really cared about legitimate international students, they would be thanking President Trump for cracking down on the rampant fraud to ensure only those truly intending to study in the United States are given the privilege."

The State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

If foreign student enrollment plummets as expected, international education advocates warn it might not bounce back the way it has from previous downturns because schools in other countries are eager to compete for these students.

Fanta Aw, executive director of NAFSA: Association of International Educators, said the visa appointment situation this summer was "even more difficult" for international students than it was during the Covid-19 pandemic, which spurred a 46% decline among those studying at a U.S. university for the first time.

"There is a very intentional attempt by this government to close the doors," Aw said, adding that prospective students "now understand that uncertainty has become the policy of this administration. … As a result, we have seen expression of interest in the U.S. decline significantly, and with students refocusing their energy on other destinations of choice."

Survey data released Thursday by NAFSA and Study Portals, a research consulting group, found that 50% of colleges in continental Europe saw higher undergraduate enrollments among international students and 59% of Asian schools saw higher postgraduate enrollments between August and October.

The DHS spokesperson said "NAFSA's 'reporting' is completely misleading and not backed up by any real evidence" and that the Student and Exchange Visitor Program "has not experienced a 10% drop of foreign student enrollment."

A significant factor for international students — especially those at the graduate level — when choosing to study in the United States is the ability to earn work experience. But the Trump administration is seeking to make that much harder, arguing that these programs have become a "back door into the American workforce" and are putting American workers at a disadvantage.

In addition to the new procedural regime, the administration is creating new pressure on the nation's foreign student enrollment with a plan announced last month to sharply raise visa fees.

The DHS has proposed a stunning $70,000 fee for each student seeking Optional Practical Training, known as OPT, which is a key driver of foreign student enrollment. Participants made up roughly a quarter of all international students in the United States.

Under the administration's proposal, universities would be responsible for paying the fees. A DHS spokesperson last month said the changes will "require foreign students to justify their worth to employers."

Higher education advocates say schools will likely pass the costs on to students. The program allows foreign students on F-1 visas to temporarily work in the United States in jobs related to their fields of study after graduation. It often serves as a bridge for those students to transition to other immigration statuses, like the H-1B visa, a temporary, employer-sponsored visa, to continue working in the country.

"We couldn't do it. It wouldn't be affordable for us to do that," said Wesleyan's Roth, whose international enrollment has held steady. "Maybe there are super-rich schools that could do that. But for a school, even a small liberal arts college, to do that for their international students who are graduating, it's going to be millions of dollars."

The Trump administration has also proposed steep fees of more than $100,000 for certain new H-1B petitions . And, among other regulatory changes, DHS finalized a separate rule in July requiring foreign students to apply for visa extensions if they need more than four years. A federal court blocked the proposal before it could take effect in September.

Veuger said additional limits could be ahead.

"You can always impose more fees. You can start suspending universities' ability to issue the documents they need to renew their visas. You can make it even harder to go get appointments," he said. "As long as there's people coming in, they can make it harder."

articles.title: A metro Atlanta woman was awarded $2.5 million by a Cobb County, Georgia jury after a 2023 rear-end crash left her with injuries so serious that she later needed spinal fusion surgery
articles.summary: A Georgia woman has been awarded $2.5 million (£1.9 million) after a rear-end collision left her with serious neck injuries and the need for spinal
articles.body: A Georgia woman has been awarded $2.5 million (£1.9 million) after a rear-end collision left her with serious neck injuries and the need for spinal surgery. A Cobb County jury reached its decision on 23 October 2026, following a case involving a crash on Cobb Parkway in 2023. The woman was represented by attorneys from Morgan & Morgan, according to WSB-TV Channel 2. The collision happened near the intersection of Cobb Parkway and Roberts Boulevard. The woman was attempting to turn right from Roberts Boulevard when she stopped to give way to approaching traffic. The vehicle behind her failed to stop and crashed into the back of her car, according to the law firm. The jury awarded her $2.5 million to compensate for the injuries and their impact on her daily life.The long road to recoveryThe crash left the woman with serious neck injuries that required several forms of medical treatment. According to WSB-TV, her treatment included injections, a DiscFX procedure and spinal fusion surgery. The injuries caused significant and ongoing pain, which affected her ability to enjoy everyday activities. Her legal team said the crash had changed her quality of life and stopped her from taking part in things she previously enjoyed. Spinal fusion is an operation that joins two or more bones in the backbone, known as vertebrae. The procedure is used to stabilise the spine and can help reduce pain caused by damaged or injured areas. According to the Cleveland Clinic, surgeons may use bone grafts, screws and metal rods to help join the bones. Recovery can take several months, and some patients may experience lasting changes in their movement and flexibility. For the woman, the need for spinal fusion meant the effects of the collision went beyond the initial injuries. Her treatment and continuing pain became important parts of the compensation case.Legal argument and damage claimThe woman was represented by Morgan & Morgan attorneys Matthew Grossman, Matthew Futrell, Austin Hollimon and Christle Guinyard. The legal team argued that the crash had caused lasting injuries and had seriously affected their client's quality of life. According to WSB-TV, the case focused on the medical treatment she needed and the continuing pain caused by the collision. Her injuries required extensive care, including injections and two procedures before and during her recovery. John Morgan, founder of Morgan & Morgan, said the legal team wanted the jury to understand how much the crash had taken away from the woman. "This case was about showing the jury what was taken from our client because of another driver's negligence," Morgan said.He added that the injuries had prevented her from enjoying activities that were important to her, including camping with her fiancé. The claim sought compensation for the physical injuries as well as the wider effects on her life. In personal injury cases, damages can cover medical expenses, lost income and other financial losses. They can also include compensation for pain, suffering and the loss of activities a person previously enjoyed. Georgia law recognises two main categories of damages:Special damages: These cover financial losses that can be calculated, such as medical bills, treatment costs and lost wages.General damages: These cover losses that are harder to measure financially, including physical pain, emotional suffering and reduced quality of life.The jury's $2.5 million award reflects the outcome of this particular case. However, the available reporting does not provide a breakdown showing how much was awarded under each category.A clear message on damagesThe verdict highlights the importance of considering the wider effects of serious injuries when deciding compensation in personal injury cases. A crash can affect more than a person's physical health. Ongoing pain, medical appointments and restrictions on everyday activities can also change how someone lives. In this case, Morgan & Morgan said the woman had lost the ability to enjoy activities that previously formed part of her daily life. Her treatment included spinal surgery, and her lawyers presented the effects of those injuries to the jury. Georgia law allows juries to decide the value of general damages based on the evidence presented during a trial. Unlike medical bills or lost wages, there is no fixed calculation for pain and suffering. The state also follows a comparative fault system. If an injured person is partly responsible for a crash, their compensation can be reduced according to their share of responsibility. A person who is found to be 50 per cent or more at fault cannot recover damages under Georgia law. Georgia generally gives people two years to file a personal injury lawsuit following an accident. The collision happened in 2023, and the jury delivered its verdict on 23 October 2026.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: After an Alabama court found a father used a false name to send harassing emails to his ex-wife, she won sole custody of their three children; appeals judges upheld her protection order but reopened visitation limits
articles.summary: A custody dispute can become more complicated when harassment between former spouses begins affecting their parenting arrangements and children's welfare.
articles.body: A custody dispute can become more complicated when harassment between former spouses begins affecting their parenting arrangements and children's welfare. In Alabama, a father who was found to have sent threatening emails to his former wife using a fictitious identity challenged a court order that gave her sole custody of their three children. The Alabama Court of Civil Appeals has now upheld the custody decision and a protection order against him, but sent the case back to reconsider how much time he can spend with the children.In a November 13, 2026 opinion, the appeals court affirmed the protection-from-abuse order and most of the lower court's custody judgment in G.W.G. v. V.M.G., available on Justia. However, it ruled that limiting the father's supervised visits to six hours every other week went further than necessary and required the trial court to establish a different visitation schedule.Dispute escalated after divorceAccording to the court's opinion, the former couple divorced in January 2023 and initially shared joint legal and physical custody of their three children. Their agreement also prohibited them from harassing each other or making derogatory comments about one another in front of the children.The mother later alleged that the father had repeatedly harassed her, prompting her to seek a custody modification and a protection-from-abuse order in November and December 2023. She requested sole legal and physical custody, saying their attempts to communicate through a parenting application and attend co-parenting counselling had failed.The dispute also involved emails sent under the name "John Tyler". The mother testified that the messages attempted to pressure her into recording an explicit video involving the father and threatened to contact her employer and report her to the Department of Human Resources if she did not comply.She said the emails contained personal information about her vehicle, including its identification number and registration details. The father initially denied sending them, but text messages admitted into evidence included his acknowledgement that he was the person behind the "John Tyler" emails. He later disputed that the message amounted to an admission of guilt.Court finds father responsible for emailsThe trial court considered the emails alongside testimony from the mother, a family therapist and a police officer. The therapist described a co-parenting session in which the father allegedly shouted and moved towards the mother, making the therapist concerned for their safety. A police officer also testified about reports concerning the father's conduct and recorded telephone conversation in which he discussed sending emails to the mother.In its January 2026 judgment, the trial court found that the father had used a fictitious identity to send the harassing messages. It also expressed concern about his fixation on the mother's relationships and whereabouts, and found that he had used visitation with the children to advance his efforts to control her.The court awarded the mother sole legal and physical custody. It ordered the father to have supervised visits every other Saturday and Sunday, for three hours each day, with supervision provided by the Bridge Center. He was also required to pay the associated costs. The father was further prohibited from going within 300 feet of the mother's residence and from arranging surveillance of her or the children through another person.Appeals court upholds protection orderThe father challenged the admission of the emails, arguing that they had not been properly authenticated and should not have been considered as evidence. The appeals court rejected this argument, pointing to his text message acknowledging that he had sent them.The judges also upheld the protection-from-abuse order, which prohibited him from contacting, harassing or stalking the mother and required him to stay away from her residence, workplace and the children's school. The order was set to remain effective until March 6, 2027. The appeals court also left the mother's sole custody arrangement intact, along with the requirement that the father pay for supervised visitation.Why judges ordered a new visitation scheduleHowever, the appeals court found that the lower court had imposed an overly restrictive visitation schedule. It noted that there was no evidence that the father had abused the children or that his conduct towards the mother had harmed their relationship with him. A visitation supervisor had also testified that the children appeared comfortable during a supervised visit and interacted positively with their father.The judges agreed that supervised visits were justified, particularly because the father had threatened to take the children to Louisiana. However, they concluded that limiting him to six hours of supervised contact every other week was not sufficiently tailored to the concerns identified by the trial court.On November 13, 2026, the Alabama Court of Civil Appeals reversed that specific visitation restriction and sent the matter back to the lower court to determine an appropriate schedule. The decision leaves the mother's sole custody and the protection order in place, while requiring the court to reconsider the father's visitation hours.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Charlamagne blasts AOC for ‘beating around the bush,’ presses progressives on backing Hakeem Jeffries
articles.summary: Charlamagne tha God called out Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez for dodging a direct challenge to Hakeem Jeffries' speaker of the House bid.
articles.body: Radio host Charlamagne tha God blasted Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., for "beating around the bush" about House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries' bid for speaker on Friday — criticizing her explanation of leadership elections instead of directly calling for a challenger. "I'm watching a lot of beating around the bush. When I see AOC do her tutorial on Instagram Live and I see her getting asked questions … What she really wants to say is, ‘I don’t think Hakeem Jeffrey should be the speaker,'" Charlamagne said during Friday’s episode of the Loud Speakers Network's "The Brilliant Idiots" podcast. "But, instead of just coming out and saying that and saying, 'Hey, I don't think he should be the speaker of the House. Somebody should challenge him,' she's kind of like beating around the bush telling people why, you know, what the process would look like," he continued. "We don't need a civics lesson." REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: A USER’S MANUAL TO UPCOMING LEADERSHIP ELECTIONS IN THE HOUSE AND SENATE The debate over Jeffries' bid has extended beyond podcast commentary to incoming lawmakers weighing their votes. Rep.-elect Adam Hamawy, D-N.J., said his support should not be taken for granted. "We're not withholding votes," Hamawy said. "What we’re doing is saying we're undecided. We’re not going to rubber-stamp anything." Other Democrats have expressed firm support for Jeffries. Rep. Wesley Bell, D-Mo., a Congressional Black Caucus member, left no uncertainty about his choice. "Hakeem Jeffries all the way," Bell said, in a statement to Fox News Digital. WHOOPI GOLDBERG LECTURES DEMOCRATS OVER INFIGHTING ABOUT LEADERSHIP, WARNS 'GET YOUR STUFF TOGETHER' Charlamagne's assessment followed a social media clip, in which Ocasio-Cortez explained how lawmakers enter leadership races. She encouraged viewers to ask whom their representatives supported rather than simply whether they opposed a particular candidate. "The question needs to be, ‘Who do you actually want for the speakership? Who is running?’ And right now, both of these races are uncontested," Ocasio-Cortez said. Charlamagne challenged whether that procedural explanation addressed progressives' disagreements with Jeffries, particularly over military assistance to Israel, and questioned how lawmakers who have described Israel’s actions in Gaza as genocide could support leaders they believe would continue those policies. "We need, ‘Hey, AOC, simple and plain. As a person, who has said Israel is committing a genocide in Gaza, how can you support leaders that you know who continue to support, in your words, the genocide?’" Charlamagne said. VAN HOLLEN CHALLENGES SCHUMER FOR SENATE LEADERSHIP AFTER DEMOCRATIC ELECTION SWEEP Ocasio-Cortez was among the lawmakers listed on a November 2025 resolution, seeking recognition of genocide in Gaza. Jeffries, who announced his speaker candidacy after the midterms, addressed divisions over Israel assistance during an interview on Wednesday, saying that lawmakers would work together to reconsider how assistance is provided. "Clearly, dramatic change is necessary," Jeffries said. "I've repeatedly made that point clear, including in July in a letter to the Caucus." articles.title: 2 cattle smugglers killed in Nuh encounter, second in a month
articles.summary: Two alleged cattle smugglers were killed and one injured in a police encounter in Nuh’s Bima village; seven cows rescued, weapons seized, magisterial inquiry ordered.
articles.body: Gurgaon: Two alleged cattle smugglers were killed and a third critically injured in an exchange of fire with police in Nuh’s Bima village early on Sunday. The suspects allegedly opened fire when a police team signalled their pickup truck to stop, prompting the cops to retaliate. A policeman was also injured in the gunfight.The men were allegedly transporting seven cows when a crime investigation agency (CIA) team from Ferozepur Jhirka intercepted them near Bima around 4.30am. According to police, the team had received a tip-off about cattle being transported illegally and set up a barricade in the area. When signalled to pull over, the truck’s occupants allegedly opened fire at the cops. Police retaliated, triggering an exchange in which all three occupants suffered bullet injuries. A constable was also hit by a bullet.The injured trio were rushed to Shaheed Hasan Khan Mewati Medical College at Nalhar, where two of them succumbed to their injuries. They were identified as Gabbar alias Hadiya, from Rajasthan’s Dausa, and Sabir. The third, Tahir, a resident of Ghatmika in Rajasthan’s Deeg district, is undergoing treatment.Tahir, police said, has 10 criminal cases registered against him, including those related to murder and cattle smuggling, while Gabbar faced a dacoity case in Nuh. Police are still checking Sabir’s criminal antecedents. “The autopsies of the deceased have been conducted. The cattle were being transported to Fondawas for delivery to a man identified as Waris, who also has four to five cases registered against him,” a police officer said.Apart from seven animals, police recovered three country-made .315-bore pistols, three live cartridges and five empty cartridge cases. The vehicle was also seized.A magisterial inquiry was initiated into the deaths. “We have kept the bodies in the mortuary and informed the families. A magisterial inquiry has been initiated into the matter,” a senior police officer said.This was the second encounter involving suspected cattle smugglers in Nuh in a month. On Oct 15, Shahid alias Advani (27), a resident of Kharkhari village in Nuh, was killed near Silani village on the Gurgaon-Nuh border. Police had intercepted his SUV around 4.30am after receiving information that it was carrying two cattle. Its occupants allegedly opened fire, following which police retaliated. Shahid died, while his two associates escaped.According to police, Advani faced more than 30 criminal cases, including those related to cattle smuggling and ATM thefts.The pattern of armed resistance surfaced in other Nuh encounters too. On Sept 20, two suspected smugglers were injured and arrested after their SUV allegedly broke through a police barricade near Ghasera village. Police said two accomplices escaped after an exchange of fire. Three cattle, two illegal firearms and seven cartridges were recovered.Earlier, on June 9, a pickup carrying five cattle allegedly breached a police blockade near Badi Kothi on the Delhi-Mumbai Expressway. During the chase, its occupants allegedly fired at a CIA team. articles.title: Wales' young carers say they need support in their role
articles.summary: Neraya says young carers such as herself want the chance of "a childhood of our own".
articles.body:
Neraya is only 15 but cannot remember a time when she was not a carer for her two sisters.

She is among the young carers crying out for what they have called crucial support, with Neraya saying she has even had to explain what she does to her teachers.

On Monday, the Welsh government will publish a national strategy for unpaid carers, which will have seven priorities including earlier recognition and mental health support.

Neraya, from Bridgend, said people in her position wanted the chance of "a childhood of our own".

Carers Wales said the strategy looked positive in parts, but it was "disappointed" manifesto promises would be excluded and raised questions over how it will be funded.

There are an estimated 5.8 million unpaid carers in the UK , 170,000 of whom are young.

The 2021 Census said this included about 120,000 carers, aged five to 17 in England and 8,200 in Wales.

Scottish government recognised there were 42,050 unpaid carers identified in the 2021-22 Carers Census.

Neraya's sisters have varying needs and she helps with practical things such as helping them get ready for school, as well as emotional support, and said there was a lack of understanding about the sacrifices young carers make.

"There's not the understanding that you might not have been able to go somewhere because we had some sort of problem within the household because my sister was ill and I'm worrying about my sister, that kind of thing," she said.

Neraya said she used to get "picked on" because people did not know what was happening with her siblings and others tended to assume they were just "naughty".

Once, in primary school, she said she was called to stand in front of her class and explain what she did because "teachers themselves didn't understand what it was".

Being a carer does not take away from her life, she said, but having support and being made to feel "valid" would give people like her "the chance to have a... childhood of our own at the same time".

The Welsh government said its strategy would focus on seven priority areas, shaped by conversations with carers with the aim of improving early recognition, access to support and respite, and better information on their rights.

It also indicated more support for mental health and wellbeing.

Reece Peachy, 17, from Ebbw Vale, Blaenau Gwent, helps care for his youngest brother while his parents support his other siblings with additional needs.

He said being a carer was "difficult but easy at the same time", but has to be home more than the average teenager.

He said: "If I have plans me and my mam will talk about it and I'll watch him. You naturally just help them out and I've been doing it for so long its just an instinct."

Reece said it could be "tough sometimes" as he balances his responsibilities with seeing friends and going to college as he puts his brother "before anything else".

"It can feel very frustrating and lonely because I wont spend much time with other people and sometimes I have to push aside things I want to do."

He said his local young carers group helped a lot by providing trips around Wales and helping him get his Duke of Edinburgh award to add to his CV.

He plans to finish his college course in carpentry before doing an apprenticeship, all while continuing to help his parents.

"I know if I move away too far they will struggle. My parents always say they are so grateful for what I do."

Cerys Morgan, 19, has helped support her 16-year-old brother, who is non-verbal and autistic, as well as being physically disabled, since she was eight.

She helps with mostly physical tasks - such as getting him ready for school and taking his medication - but also provides emotional support.

"I've developed an understanding more than I think other people would as a sister," she said.

"I understand how he's feeling, what his needs are and how I can support him if he's having a hard day or a happy day and know what's best for him, in that way as being a sister, to support him."

She called emotional support for young carers "really important" in order to help them develop skills and resilience in their roles, especially those who find themselves in the role at a young age.

"When I was eight I didn't understand what a young carer meant," she said.

She suggested the Welsh government could look at mentor schemes to link young people up - something she wished she had "when I was little to support me and for me to communicate with as well".

Deputy minister for social care, Delyth Jewell, described unpaid carers as the "backbone of care" across Wales.

But Carers Wales said the strategy does not go far enough.

Head of external affairs Rob Simkins said: "There are some welcome parts of the new strategy, particularly around access to respite care and a desire to see more carers receiving support.

"However, it is not clear how the government intends to make the step-change needed without additional investment to provide the extra support that unpaid carers desperately need.

"It is also disappointing that the manifesto commitment to ensuring carers' needs assessments are completed within 28 days is missing from the strategy."

He said the organisation wanted to make sure unpaid carers lives are better and was not sure that this strategy "will go as far as we want it to".

The Welsh government said: "We have engaged extensively with a wide range of social care groups and our national strategy for unpaid carers will help ensure they get the recognition and support they deserve.

"We are considering whether changes are needed to strengthen support for carers, including imposing a timescale on the completion of carers' needs assessments."

articles.title: Empty Vande Bharat allowed to run 463km despite 'poor power brake'
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: An empty Vande Bharat train was allowed to travel around 463km from Hatia in Jharkhand to Deen Dayal Upadhyaya station in UP despite two loco
articles.body: NEW DELHI: An empty Vande Bharat train was allowed to travel around 463km from Hatia in Jharkhand to Deen Dayal Upadhyaya station in UP despite two loco pilots reporting "poor power brake". An inspection subsequently found that the brakes on every coach had been isolated, "resulting in non-application of joint brakes."The incident happened on Oct 24, as per a document of South Eastern Railway, and posed a potential risk to other passenger trains. In a Nov 7 order, the zone directed Ranchi divisional railway manager to investigate the incident "to ascertain the lapses on part of staff concerned" for taking necessary steps.It highlighted failures on part of staff members. As per the document, instructions were issued on Oct 24 for a freight locomotive to haul the empty Vande Bharat chair car rake from Hatia to Jhansi. News agency PTI, quoting officials, said staff were supposed to integrate the rake's braking system with that of the locomotive for the entire journey.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Lalit gets British citizenship, extradition prospects take a hit
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: IPL founder Lalit Modi, who left India in 2010 amid allegations of tax evasion, money laundering and proxy ownership linked to IPL, has
articles.body: NEW DELHI: IPL founder Lalit Modi, who left India in 2010 amid allegations of tax evasion, money laundering and proxy ownership linked to IPL, has announced he has received British citizenship, reports Rajshekhar Jha.Lalit was appearing at an event at Oxford Union when he made the announcement.Sources said while the citizenship doesn't grant him legal immunity or formally stop his extradition under the 1992 India-UK treaty, it might have diminished, if not eliminated, the chances of his return. Efforts to bring him back will continue, sources said. Receiving UK nationality also closes the door on potential moves like deportation, leaving formal extradition as India's sole legal route. UK citizens who were brought to India to face trial include AgustaWestland scam accused Christian Michel and bookie Sanjeev Chawla.In ’12, UK cited local laws to reject India’s plea for Lalit’s deportationIn a post on X on Saturday, the 62-year-old revealed that he celebrated his citizenship with family and friends at a special ceremony on September 15. Calling the UK his long-time home, he expressed deep admiration for Britain's people, institutions, traditions and values.“Becoming British is a privilege and a responsibility that I embrace with pride, gratitude and a genuine sense of belonging. My life’s journey has been shaped by different cultures and experiences, and I look forward to continuing to contribute positively to the country I proudly call home,” he wrote, thanking the Oxford Union and signing off with, “God Save the King!”Modi has refused to return to India, citing threats from the ‘underworld’ and other quarters. He has also claimed to be the target of a political witch-hunt, which stalled the issuance of a Red Notice by Interpol.In 2015, the CBI had sent documents to Interpol seeking a notice against him, and a non-bailable warrant was issued against him in Mumbai. Modi then applied for citizenship in the Caribbean tax haven of Saint Lucia through an investment scheme, following which the local Interpol unit there sought documents from India.According to the Enforcement Directorate (ED), Modi manipulated the process of assigning broadcast rights for the IPL in 2009, allegedly in exchange for a kickback of over Rs 125 crore. The ED's money laundering case followed an FIR registered against him by the Central Crime Branch of Tamil Nadu Police on October 13, 2010.The ED had Modi's passport revoked by the Regional Passport Office in Mumbai on March 3, 2011. It was later restored on the directions of the Delhi High Court. In November 2012, the UK government was formally requested to deport him to India, but the request was denied on December 21, 2012, citing domestic laws. The ED had also sent a letter of request to the UK for the execution of the non-bailable warrant against him.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Police ban protests near 10 schools and five universities in Paris
articles.summary: The order will be in place from 16 to 20 November, Paris police chief Patrice Faure says.
articles.body:
Police in Paris have issued a five-day ban on protests near 10 secondary schools and five universities as authorities try to control weeks of blockades and violence at educational venues in France.

The order prohibits unauthorised gatherings or marches within 100m of the sites from 16 to 20 November.

Paris police chief Patrice Faure said the ban was necessary due to "numerous disruptions and blockades around certain secondary schools and establishments of higher learning" and "persistent violence".

A wave of protests began in France September over poor secondary school conditions, before spreading to universities, workers and a "yellow-vest" movement against the cost of living.

Announcing the order, the Paris police chief said blockades around certain secondary schools and universities have led to damaged public property, violence against members of the educational community and clashes with law enforcement.

Mayors of eight Parisian districts had contacted the regional education authority to call for measures to "secure the entrances and exits" of blockaded secondary schools, local media report.

Some 1,548 people have been arrested in Paris since the start of the protests, Faure said on Sunday.

On Saturday, 106,000 people from a range of groups took to the streets in France, including 24,000 in Paris, the interior ministry said.

It marked the fifth Saturday in a row where students, unions and yellow-vest activists went out to protest.

The number of protesters was much lower than previously, and so was the number of those arrested, the ministry said - 219 across the country, including 45 in Paris.
