articles.title: A 200-year-old roof tile found at a UK salvage yard carries a handwritten dismissal message to a worker named John Lewis, possibly linking it to an 1820 Staffordshire brickmaking business
articles.summary: A handwritten message believed to be about 200 years old has been discovered on a Staffordshire Blue roof tile at a salvage yard in Rugeley, Staffordshire.
articles.body: A handwritten message believed to be about 200 years old has been discovered on a Staffordshire Blue roof tile at a salvage yard in Rugeley, Staffordshire. The inscription appears to record the dismissal of a worker named John Lewis by someone called Thomas Austin. It was written into soft clay before the tile was fired, preserving the words through about two centuries of use on a roof.According to the BBC, the tile was found at Cawarden Reclaim, where staff recognised its possible historical importance. Research identified a business called Thomas Austin Brick & Tile Makers at Clay Hills, Stoke-on-Trent, in 1820.A 200-year-old dismissal message found on a Staffordshire roof tileThe inscription was found on a Staffordshire Blue roof tile at Cawarden Reclaim, a salvage yard in Rugeley. It reads, “I do hereby discharge you, John Lewis, from my employment, Thomas Austin.” The message appears to be a written notice that Lewis was no longer employed.The words had been written into soft clay before the tile was fired, leaving them preserved on the finished roofing material. The yard describes the tile as about 200 years old.What does the inscription on the old tile reveal about its historyGeneral manager Adam Giles said, "We were looking around and we just happened to come across this tile.”He took it back to the yard, cleaned it, and quickly felt it had historical significance. The company said the name, location, and period made a potential connection, based on its research into a business identified in 1820.The company conceded it did not know for certain that the two were linked. The company had found a firm called Thomas Austin Brick & Tile Makers, based at Clay Hills, Stoke-on-Trent, in 1820. Giles said, "If it is the same person [Thomas Austin], we may have uncovered not only a glimpse into somebody's working life in the early 19th century, but also a connection to the people who made the very building materials that have survived to this day."What makes this historic roofing tile an unusual discoveryGiles said, "You come across quite a few pawprints from animals and old shoes, where they used to walk across the clay while they were being fired.”However, he said handwritten text on a tile was much less common. He described the discovery as very unusual and rare. The inscription was made before the clay was fired, and the finished tile was later used for its intended purpose as roofing material.Giles said, "The fact that someone went to the trouble of writing that out on the back of clay before it was fired, and then firing the tile and using it for the purpose it was designed for.”Why the salvage company wants to preserve its unusual discoveriesCawarden Reclaim said it found intriguing items such as this from time to time. When staff found items considered noteworthy, they kept them aside and preserved them. The company said these objects would eventually be displayed in its reception area as part of a wall of interest. The tile’s inscription appears to record a direct message from an employer to a named worker, but the circumstances behind the dismissal are not known from the discovery. Nor has the company confirmed that the Thomas Austin named in the message was linked to the Stoke-on-Trent brick and tile business.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Those using Form 6 to re-enroll won't be prosecuted: EC to SC
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Election Commission has assured Supreme Court that all attempts will be made to include every eligible citizen in the electoral rolls and
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Election Commission has assured Supreme Court that all attempts will be made to include every eligible citizen in the electoral rolls and no prosecution would be launched against people whose names were deleted from the post-SIR draft electoral rolls, for using Form 6 for restoration of their names in the voters' lists.EC's stand, spelt out in an affidavit filed Saturday, is in sync with the Oct 26 assurance given by a bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana while hearing petitions relating to alleged large-scale deletion of voters in Maharashtra and Delhi. The CJI-led bench had said, "No one will be prosecuted for filling Form 6 seeking re-entering of their names in voters' lists."Petitioners had highlighted voters' apprehension that they might be prosecuted for giving a false declaration in Form 6, which is used for enrolling new voters, that they had never been registered as voters before.Errors likely in weeding out dead, non-existent voters: ECEC said, "No prosecution will be launched against anyone for filing Form 6 merely on the ground that the applicant/elector was previously enrolled in the electoral roll(s) prior to the SIR and their names did not appear in the draft electoral rolls during the SIR."However, EC said those filling Form 6 to restore their names in the electoral rolls must ensure their names do not figure in the voters' lists in any other assembly or parliamentary constituency.Assuring the court that efforts have been intensified to register every eligible citizen as a voter, EC said, "A mechanism has also been directed to be put in place to ensure that no elector is deprived of the opportunity to get his/her name included in the final electoral roll, subject to fulfilment of the prescribed eligibility conditions, while taking due care to avoid duplication in enrolment."Accepting that there may have been errors in weeding out non-existent and dead voters from the electoral rolls through SIR, the commission said, "There are challenges on count of the large numbers involved, and also because the full data is being digitised. There have been and will be problems that arise from time to time and the commission remains alive to the need to ensure that all those who are eligible to vote find their name in the voters' lists but equally, to ensure that all inconsistencies in these lists are addressed."On complaints about large-scale deletion of voters in Delhi through SIR in the ASDD (absent, shifted, duplicate and dead) category, EC said those left out of the draft electoral rolls could submit fresh enumeration forms to electoral registration officers or assistant EROs at their current residential place."Electors who have not shifted may submit the signed enumeration form with the statement giving the reason for the earlier non-submission of the enumeration form. They can submit it to the ERO/AERO/BLO in person or through family members. Online submission option with e-sign will be available on ECINET," it said.Those Delhi voters who have shifted residence from one constituency to another can submit fresh enumeration forms along with address proof to the ERO/AERO or avail the option of 'book a call with BLO', it said."Enumeration forms submitted by such electors shall be processed by EROs in accordance with Rule 21(1) of Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, and the same EPIC number shall be re-assigned to them. An elector who has already submitted Form 6 during the SIR need not submit the enumeration form afresh," EC said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
